title: THE WOMAN JESUS CALLED “JEZEBEL”: THE SIN A CHURCH LEARNED TO TOLERATE—UNTIL CHRIST HIMSELF CONFRONTED IT
paragraphs: THE WOMAN JESUS CALLED “JEZEBEL”: THE SIN A CHURCH LEARNED TO TOLERATE—UNTIL CHRIST HIMSELF CONFRONTED IT

She was accused of leading believers into sexual immorality and idolatry. But the most terrifying part of Revelation 2:20–23 isn't what this woman was doing. It's what Jesus saw happening inside a church that still thought it belonged to Him.
Imagine walking into a church where the worship is beautiful.
The songs are moving. The people know Scripture. Someone is praying with tears streaming down their face. The congregation speaks passionately about love, acceptance, and spiritual freedom.
Everything looks alive.
But somewhere beneath the worship, something is dying.

A compromise has become a habit. A habit has become a teaching. And a teaching has become so familiar that people no longer recognize the difference between the voice of Jesus and the voice of someone using His name.
Then comes a message.
Not from an angry outsider.
Not from someone trying to destroy the church.
But from Jesus Christ Himself.
And His words are devastating.
“But I have this against you…”
Imagine hearing those words from the Savior who died for you.
Not because He has stopped loving you.
But because He loves you too much to pretend that what is destroying you is harmless.
This is the frightening, heartbreaking, and ultimately hope-filled story behind the woman called “Jezebel” in Revelation 2:20–23.
And before you decide this story is about somebody else's sin, somebody else's church, or somebody else's scandal, consider something.
The woman is not the only person Jesus confronts.
He also confronts those who have learned to tolerate what He calls them to reject.
And that brings this ancient warning dangerously close to our own hearts.
The setting is Thyatira, a city in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Türkiye.

The risen Christ addresses a real Christian congregation there. This is not a fictional courtroom scene or a story invented to frighten believers. It is part of the message recorded in Revelation, written to seven churches facing spiritual pressures, temptations, suffering, and compromise.
Before confronting Thyatira's sin, Jesus acknowledges something beautiful.
“I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first.” (Revelation 2:19, KJV)
Think about that.
This church was not described as completely inactive or devoid of faith.
There was love.
There was service.
There was perseverance.
There was evidence of growth.
Yet spiritual activity had not eliminated spiritual danger.
A congregation can be busy serving Jesus while failing to confront something that dishonors Him.
A person can appear spiritually mature in one area while quietly surrendering another area of life to sin.
And then Jesus identifies the problem.

“Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.” (Revelation 2:20, KJV)
Read that again.
Jesus did not merely condemn a woman's private behavior.
He confronted teaching that was leading His servants into sin.
And He confronted the church for allowing it.
The word translated “sufferest” in the King James Version means allow or tolerate in this context.
The underlying Greek verb is ἀφεῖς (apheis), from aphiēmi, which can mean to permit or allow.
Jesus was saying, in effect, that the congregation was allowing a destructive influence to continue among His people.
And the name He used carried a terrible history.
Jezebel.
To understand why that name mattered, we must return centuries earlier to the Old Testament.
In 1 Kings 16–21, Jezebel was the wife of King Ahab of Israel. She promoted Baal worship, opposed the prophets of the LORD, and played a central role in the injustice that resulted in Naboth's death.
Her story became a lasting biblical picture of idolatry, corrupt influence, and hostility toward God's truth.
But here is an important distinction.
Revelation does not tell us that the woman in Thyatira was literally the same Jezebel from the Old Testament. Centuries separated them.
Nor can we establish with certainty whether “Jezebel” was her actual name or a symbolic designation used to describe her resemblance to the infamous queen.
What Scripture does tell us is that this woman claimed prophetic authority and was influencing believers toward sexual immorality and participation in food associated with idol worship.
We must not invent her biography.
We do not know her appearance, her family history, the precise words of her teachings, or every method she used to gain influence.
But we know enough to understand the warning.
Someone claiming to speak with spiritual authority was teaching people to embrace behavior Jesus condemned.
And some believers were listening.
Perhaps that is what makes the passage so uncomfortable.
False teaching does not always arrive announcing itself as rebellion against God.
Sometimes it arrives wrapped in religious vocabulary.
Sometimes it offers permission where Scripture calls for repentance.
Sometimes it tells people that obedience is unnecessary, that compromise is harmless, or that spiritual maturity means moving beyond inconvenient commands.
It may sound compassionate.
It may sound sophisticated.
It may even sound liberating.
But any message that teaches people to make peace with sin is not freedom in Christ.
It is another form of bondage.
And bondage does not become holy simply because someone attaches God's name to it.
The Greek text of Revelation 2:20 uses two especially revealing expressions.
διδάσκει καὶ πλανᾷ — didaskei kai plana.
They mean “she teaches and leads astray.”
This is important.
The passage describes more than a person struggling privately with temptation.
It describes a corrupting influence that was being taught and spread.
There is a profound difference between a believer who falls into sin and grieves over it, and a teacher who persuades others that they need not repent of it.
Both need the mercy of Christ.
But the second can lead many others into destruction.
The passage also names the sins involved.
πορνεῦσαι (porneusai) refers to committing sexual immorality.
εἰδωλόθυτα (eidōlothyta) refers to things sacrificed to idols.
These are not vague accusations that we are free to redefine according to personal preference.
They concern sexual wrongdoing and idolatrous compromise.

In the ancient world, religious, economic, and social activities could overlap. Thyatira was associated with commercial trades and guilds, and scholars have suggested that pressures surrounding communal meals and pagan practices may help explain the temptation facing believers there.
That historical possibility is worth considering.
But Revelation does not specify the exact gatherings or circumstances involved, so we should not pretend to know more than the text reveals.
What is clear is that Christians were being drawn toward practices incompatible with their allegiance to Christ.
And Jesus was not indifferent.
Now imagine the personal cost of obedience.
What if refusing to participate meant losing opportunities?
What if remaining faithful made you unpopular?
What if the people around you insisted that you were taking Christianity too seriously?
What if compromise offered an easier path?
Suddenly this ancient church begins to look remarkably familiar.
Because temptation rarely presents itself as a request to destroy your life.
It often asks for one small exception.
Just this once.
Just this relationship.
Just this secret.
Just this compromise.
Just this thing everybody else is doing.
And then another.
Until the heart becomes comfortable with what once troubled the conscience.
Perhaps someone reading this knows that progression intimately.
You remember when a particular sin used to grieve you.
You remember when conviction came quickly.
You remember when you could not sleep without praying about it.
But after repeating it, excusing it, and hiding it, something changed.
The sin did not become less serious.
Your resistance became weaker.
And somewhere along the way, you began calling your surrender peace.
That is a dangerous place to live.
Not because Jesus has become unwilling to forgive.
But because we can become increasingly unwilling to admit that we need forgiveness.
Yet the next words of Jesus reveal something astonishing.
Something that should make every struggling sinner stop reading for a moment.
“And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not.” (Revelation 2:21, KJV)
Do you see it?
Before the announced judgment, there was an opportunity to repent.
Before the warning reached its most terrifying point, Jesus revealed that time had been given.
The Greek expression is ἔδωκα αὐτῇ χρόνον ἵνα μετανοήσῃ — edōka autē chronon hina metanoēsē.
It means, “I gave her time so that she might repent.”
The verb metanoeō refers to repentance—a change of mind and direction, turning away from sin toward God.
This is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what you did.
It is not regretting the consequences while secretly protecting the behavior.
Biblical repentance involves recognizing sin for what it is and turning toward the Lord in faith and obedience.
And Jesus gave her time.
Let those words reach the places you have been trying to hide.
Jesus gave her time.
The One whose eyes are described in Revelation 2:18 as being like a flame of fire was not ignorant of her actions.
He saw.
He knew.
He confronted.
And still, there was an opportunity to turn.
What a revelation of both His holiness and His patience.
The Lord who refuses to call evil good is also the Lord who calls sinners to repentance.
But the verse ends with a heartbreaking statement.
“And she repented not.”
Not because the passage says repentance was impossible.
Not because Jesus offered no warning.
But because she refused to turn.
There is something especially tragic about a person becoming so committed to defending a sin that even an opportunity for repentance is rejected.
And perhaps this is where the story stops being merely about Jezebel.
Because many of us know what it feels like to argue with conviction.
We know what it is to defend something we would once have confessed.
We know how to explain away a compromise.
We know how to appear spiritually strong while carrying a private contradiction.
A married person may be feeding an emotional relationship that is slowly becoming unfaithfulness.
A young believer may be hiding a pattern of sexual behavior that contradicts the faith they profess.
A church leader may be protecting a reputation instead of acknowledging wrongdoing.
A Christian may be placing money, approval, pleasure, or personal ambition above obedience to God.
And someone may be using the language of grace to avoid the call to repentance.
These are not identical situations, and we must not accuse everyone who struggles of being like the false teacher in Thyatira.
But every one of us needs to examine what we are allowing to rule our hearts.
Because grace was never intended to become permission to remain enslaved.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic: “God forbid.”
Grace does not make sin harmless.
Grace brings us to the Savior who breaks sin's claim over us.
And now the message to Thyatira grows more severe.
“Behold, I will cast her into a bed, and them that commit adultery with her into great tribulation, except they repent of their deeds.” (Revelation 2:22, KJV)
The language is deliberately forceful.
The bed associated with wrongdoing becomes part of an image of judgment.
The warning is not a license for readers to identify suffering people as recipients of divine punishment.
It is Christ's specific prophetic warning to those involved in the wrongdoing described in this passage.
Notice, however, that even here the words “except they repent” appear.
The warning still contains a call to turn.
Then comes one of the most difficult statements in the passage.

“And I will kill her children with death; and all the churches shall know that I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts: and I will give unto every one of you according to your works.” (Revelation 2:23, KJV)
We should not soften this verse until it loses its seriousness.
Neither should we use it recklessly.

The expression translated “her children” may refer to those who follow or belong to her corrupt teaching. Interpreters differ about whether the language is figurative or refers to literal offspring. The passage does not give us enough information to identify them with certainty.
What is unmistakable is the gravity of Christ's warning.
He will judge evil.
And He knows the truth beneath outward appearances.
The Greek says:
ἐραυνῶν νεφροὺς καὶ καρδίας — eraunōn nephrous kai kardias.
Literally, “searching kidneys and hearts.”
That may sound strange to modern ears.
But in ancient biblical imagery, the kidneys, or inward parts, could represent the deepest inner life, while the heart represented the center of thought, desire, and intention.
The meaning is profound.
Jesus searches what is hidden within us.
He sees beyond reputation.
Beyond performance.
Beyond carefully chosen words.
Beyond the version of ourselves we present to others.
He knows the motives we conceal and the desires we struggle to admit.
And that truth should humble every person who claims to belong to Him.
Because you can hide a conversation from your spouse.
You can hide a browser history from your family.
You can hide dishonesty from your employer.
You can hide a secret habit from your church.
You can even convince people that everything is fine.
But you cannot hide your heart from Jesus Christ.
And here is the part that should bring us to our knees.
The One who sees everything is also the One who went to the cross to save sinners.
He does not need our deception.
He calls us into the light.
And the light is not the enemy of a repentant heart.
It is where healing begins.
Think of the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers wanted to use her sin as a weapon.
Jesus exposed their hypocrisy and refused to join their condemnation.
But He did not tell her that sin no longer mattered.
He told her to go and sin no more.

The passage has a well-known textual history and is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John's Gospel, so it should not carry the entire weight of our understanding of grace and repentance.
Yet its portrayal of mercy joined with a call to holiness is consistent with the wider New Testament.
Think also of Peter.
He denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had promised loyalty collapsed under fear.
And after the rooster crowed, Peter wept bitterly.
His failure was real.
His grief was real.
But his story did not end in the courtyard of denial.
In John 21, the risen Jesus restored Peter to a life of service.
The man who had denied Christ was called again to shepherd His sheep.
That is what makes the Gospel so extraordinary.
Jesus does not pretend that sin never happened.
He redeems people who could never erase it themselves.
And consider the apostle Paul.
Before becoming a preacher of Christ, he persecuted the church.
He carried a history that could not be undone by a better public image.
Yet he testified that he had received mercy.
The grace of God did not make Paul's former violence acceptable.
It transformed the direction of his life.
That is the difference between excusing sin and being redeemed from it.
One asks God to leave us unchanged.
The other surrenders to the Savior who makes us new.
And perhaps you have been afraid to surrender because you believe that if everything hidden were exposed, nobody would love you anymore.
Maybe you have been carrying guilt for years.
Maybe your marriage has been wounded by betrayal.
Maybe pornography has become a secret prison.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending that your relationship with God is healthy when you know your heart has drifted.
Maybe you have been hurt by a spiritual leader who used authority to excuse wrongdoing.
Maybe you were taught that asking honest questions was rebellion.
Maybe someone used the word “Jezebel” to humiliate you, silence you, or dismiss you simply because you were a woman who spoke up.
If that happened, understand this clearly.
Revelation 2 does not authorize Christians to label women “Jezebel” merely because they are outspoken, influential, disagree with a leader, or challenge wrongdoing.
The passage concerns identifiable false teaching and conduct that led believers into sin.
It is not a weapon for controlling women or silencing legitimate concerns.
A church that condemns sexual immorality while protecting sexual abuse has not understood the holiness of Christ.
A leader who invokes Scripture to escape accountability has not earned the right to silence the wounded.
Jesus is not honored when His Word is used to conceal evil.
He is honored when truth is spoken, the vulnerable are protected, wrongdoers are held accountable, and repentance bears genuine fruit.
And for anyone who has been wounded by spiritual manipulation, the answer is not to return blindly to an unsafe situation.
You can seek safety, wise counsel, and appropriate help while continuing to seek Christ.
Because the voice of the Good Shepherd is not the voice of an abuser.
He does not need manipulation to establish His authority.
He is the truth.
Now return to Thyatira.
There is another detail many people overlook.
Jesus does not treat every believer in the church as though they are equally guilty.
In Revelation 2:24–25, He addresses those who have not accepted the corrupt teaching and urges them to hold fast to what they have until He comes.
That matters.
Because the message is not simply, “Everything is corrupt, and everyone is condemned.”
It is also a call for faithful believers to endure.
Not everyone had surrendered.
Not everyone had believed the deception.
And even in a compromised congregation, Christ knew those who remained faithful.
He knew their struggle.
He knew their perseverance.
He knew their refusal to bow.
Just as He knows yours.
Perhaps you are fighting a temptation nobody else understands.
Perhaps you are choosing integrity while watching dishonesty get rewarded.
Perhaps you are remaining sexually faithful in a culture that treats commitment as disposable.
Perhaps you are refusing to join in wrongdoing even though it costs you friendships, influence, or opportunity.
Jesus sees that too.
He does not only search hidden sins.
He also knows hidden faithfulness.
And the message to Thyatira ultimately points beyond its scandal to the authority and victory of Jesus Christ.
Revelation 22:16 identifies Jesus Himself as “the bright and morning star.”
The final hope of the Christian is not merely escaping a scandal.
It is belonging to Christ.
Knowing Him.
Being made new by Him.
And sharing in the life He gives.
That is why this story cannot end with Jezebel.
It must end with Jesus.
Because Jezebel represents the deadly seriousness of corrupting compromise.
But Jesus reveals the holy mercy that calls sinners to turn before judgment.
And the cross shows us how costly that mercy truly is.
At Calvary, Jesus did not negotiate with sin.
He bore its consequences on behalf of sinners.
He, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for us.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is not cheap forgiveness.
It is blood-bought grace.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not something we earn by our works.
And Ephesians 2:10 immediately reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the beautiful balance?
We are not saved because we become good enough.
We are saved by God's grace, and that grace begins transforming the way we live.
Repentance does not purchase forgiveness.
Christ has paid the price.
Repentance is part of turning to the One who forgives and restores.
And this is why we must be careful never to turn spiritual giving into another kind of bondage.
Your salvation cannot be purchased with a donation.
Your place in God's family is not determined by how much money you give to a ministry.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
Not a payment.
Not a platform.
Not a religious organization.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
Giving that honors God is not extracted through fear or guilt.
It flows from a willing heart.
Some are battling temptation.
Some are recovering from spiritual wounds.
Some are trying to understand the Bible for the first time.
Some have almost given up on their faith.
And some are one honest encounter with the Gospel away from beginning a new journey with Christ.
It can be one practical expression of your desire to glorify God by helping make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources more accessible.
This is not a replacement for every believer's responsibility to support their local church, nor should it automatically be treated as the biblical tithe.
It is an opportunity to give willingly toward a ministry you believe is serving Christ faithfully.
It is participating in work intended to point people back to Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not reserved for those who can afford to give.
We want people to have access to biblical nourishment whether they are able to contribute financially or not.
And there is another way to help that costs nothing.
Not because every post needs to go viral.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
But because someone in your circle may need to hear that compromise is dangerous, repentance is possible, and Jesus has not stopped calling sinners to Himself.
Maybe a friend needs this reminder.
Maybe a family member has quietly drifted from faith.
Maybe someone you know has been hurt by a church and needs to hear that Jesus is not the same as the people who misrepresented Him.
There is room to ask questions.
Room to learn.
Room to wrestle honestly with Scripture.
And always, the invitation to turn toward Jesus.
But before you leave, I want to ask you something more personal.
Not as a public performance.
Not to force you to reveal a private sin.
Not to make you feel ashamed in front of strangers.
Just an honest question between your conscience and the Lord.
What have you been calling harmless that Jesus has been calling you to surrender?
Maybe you already know.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has been convicting you for a long time.
Maybe you have been postponing a difficult confession.
Maybe you need to end a relationship that is leading you away from Christ.
Maybe you need to seek help for a destructive habit.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you have harmed.
Maybe you need to stop defending what Scripture has clearly confronted.
Or maybe your next step is simply to fall on your knees and pray the prayer you have been avoiding.
“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot justify it anymore. Please forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to walk in Your truth.”
You do not need an impressive speech.
You need an honest heart turned toward the Savior.
You can simply write “Christ is still healing me.”
Or “Pray for me.”
Or share a testimony of how Jesus brought you out of compromise and into a renewed walk with Him.
You do not have to disclose details that should remain private.
Your honest words may encourage someone else who thought they were the only person still struggling.
Because the church should never become a place where everyone pretends to be perfect.
It should be a people who confess that Jesus Christ is perfect, that His grace is sufficient, and that His truth calls us into a transformed life.
And perhaps that is the greatest lesson of Thyatira.
The danger was not simply that a woman taught what was false.
It was that people could become comfortable with falsehood while still surrounded by the language and activity of faith.
But the hope was not found in pretending the problem did not exist.
It was found in the voice of the risen Christ.
The same Lord who said, “I have this against you,” also called His people to repentance and faithfulness.
He did not abandon His holiness to show mercy.
And He did not abandon His mercy to defend holiness.
Both meet perfectly in Him.
So if you have wandered, come back.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have been deceived, return to Scripture.
If you have been wounded, seek healing in truth.
If you have remained faithful through costly trials, hold fast.
And if you think your past is too scandalous for the grace of God, look again at the cross.
The cross does not tell you that your sin was insignificant.
It tells you that the Savior's love was greater than the cost He willingly bore to redeem sinners.
The empty tomb tells you that death did not defeat Him.
And His living Word still calls people out of darkness into His marvelous light.
The woman called Jezebel was given time to repent.
The passage tells us she refused.
But you are reading this message now.
And the invitation of the Gospel is still before you.
Do not confuse God's patience with His approval of sin.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
And do not mistake the temporary comfort of compromise for the lasting freedom found in Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that Jesus knows the truth about your life.
The greatest tragedy would be hearing His call and choosing to remain hidden.
The Savior who sees the sin you cannot hide is the same Savior whose nail-scarred hands are sufficient to receive the sinner who finally comes into the light.
